transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I suppose the thing that finally made me come in is that I’ve been having these mornings where I wake up and, before I’ve even really started the day, I think… it might just be easier if I hadn’t woken up at all. And that frightened me, because I don’t usually say things like that, even to myself.

I want to be clear, I don’t have some plan to hurt myself or anything like that. It’s more like this heavy thought that shows up, especially in the morning, and it scared me enough that I thought I shouldn’t just keep brushing it aside or pretending it’s nothing. So… that’s why I’m here.
How long have you been having these thoughts about not wanting to wake up in the morning?

About a month now, I think. It started after my sister died unexpectedly. I remember in the days right after, everything felt unreal, like I was just moving through the motions, and then those thoughts started coming in the mornings—when the house was quiet and I’d first wake up. So… yes, about a month.
Have you noticed any changes in your interest in activities that you normally enjoy since your sister passed away?

Yes… yes, I have. I mean, I still go through the motions. I still make myself show up for things, like my book club, because I know if I stop going it will be harder to start again. And there’s a dance night I used to really look forward to—not that I’m a wonderful dancer or anything, but it was fun, it got me out of the house, people laughed, there was music. Lately I’ll be there, and I’m physically in the room, but it feels like I’m behind a pane of glass somehow. Like everyone else is enjoying it and I’m watching it happen from somewhere else.

And at home too… my garden used to give me such a little boost. I’d fuss over the plants and feel proud when something bloomed. Cooking for the neighbors was the same way—I liked feeding people, dropping something off, feeling useful, I suppose. But now I do those things and they don’t give me that little lift they used to. I keep thinking, “Maybe if I just do it, the feeling will come back,” but so far it mostly just feels… flat.
Have you noticed any change in your weight since your sister passed away?

Yes… a little, I think. I haven’t been weighing myself carefully, so I can’t give you an exact number, but my clothes feel a bit looser.

It’s more that food just doesn’t call to me the way it used to. I’ll think, “I should eat something,” and make a piece of toast or maybe a small bowl of soup, and then somehow the whole day slips by and by evening I realize I’ve barely had anything. I’m not trying to lose weight—I’m not dieting or anything like that. It just feels like eating takes more effort than it should, and nothing sounds very appealing.
Have you noticed any changes in how active or restless you feel compared to before your sister passed away?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed that, exactly. I mean… I don’t think I’ve been pacing around or feeling like I can’t sit still, if that’s what you mean. And I don’t think I’ve become especially slowed down either, at least not in a way I’ve clearly recognized.

Some days I move a bit more slowly just because I don’t feel very motivated, but I couldn’t say it’s a real change in my activity level. I still get up and do the basic things I need to do. Maybe I’m less energetic, but not restless, no… not that I’ve noticed.
Have you been feeling guilty about anything or like you're worthless since your sister passed away?

Yes… yes, I have. I don’t know if I’d say I feel worthless all the time, exactly, but I do get caught in these loops where I go back over the last weeks with my sister again and again. I keep thinking I should have called more often, or stayed on the phone longer when I did call, or asked better questions instead of just chatting about ordinary things.

And then I tell myself I should have listened better, noticed something, done something more useful somehow. I know, rationally, part of me knows I couldn’t have changed what happened. I do know that. But there’s this other part that keeps saying, “You were her sister, you should have done more.” It’s hard to quiet that down.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than you used to, physically, since your sister passed away?

I don’t think so… not in any obvious way. I mean, I may take longer to get started with things, like I’ll sit for a while before I get up and do whatever needs doing, but once I’m actually moving around, I don’t think I’m physically slower, exactly.

No one has said anything to me like, “You’re moving differently,” and I haven’t noticed myself shuffling or speaking more slowly or anything like that. It’s more that things feel heavier to begin, if that makes sense. But physically moving more slowly than before… I can’t really say I’ve noticed that.
Do you feel like you have been fidgeting or feeling restless more often since your sister passed away?

No, I don’t think so. Not fidgeting, really. I mean, I might shift around in a chair if I’m uncomfortable or if I’ve been sitting too long, but I wouldn’t say I’ve had that restless feeling, like I need to get up and pace or keep moving.

Since my sister passed, I’ve felt unsettled emotionally, if that makes sense, but not physically restless. I’m not wringing my hands or tapping my feet all the time or unable to sit still. If anything, I tend to just sit with things for too long. But fidgeting more often… no, I haven’t really noticed that.
Have your mornings where you think it might be easier if you hadn't woken up been happening every day for the past month?

Not every single day, no… I don’t want to make it sound more precise than it is. It’s not like I wake up every morning and have the exact same thought at the exact same intensity.

But it has been happening enough that it frightened me. There are mornings when I open my eyes and before I’ve even really started the day, I’ll think, almost like a heavy sigh in my head, that maybe it would have been easier if I just hadn’t woken up. And then I get scared of myself for even thinking that.

I don’t have a plan to hurt myself. I’m not sitting there planning anything or deciding to do something. It’s more that the thought comes in as this tired, hopeless kind of feeling. But the fact that it keeps coming back — that’s what scared me enough to ask for help.
Have you felt like you're doing things in slow motion or that your thoughts are slower than they used to be since your sister passed away?

Yes… not so much like my body is in slow motion, but my thinking, yes. That’s been bothering me.

I’ll sit down with something I used to be able to handle pretty routinely, like my budgeting spreadsheet, and I’ll just stare at the same numbers and cells and it’s like they don’t quite connect in my head. I know what the spreadsheet is for, I know I’ve done it before, but I’ll look at it and then realize I haven’t actually understood what I’m looking at.

Or if I’m reading something for the workshop, I’ll reread the same paragraph three or four times, and even then I sometimes can’t tell you what it said. It’s not that the words are blurry or anything like that. It’s more like they don’t sink in. I’ll get to the end of the paragraph and think, “Wait, what did I just read?” and then I feel embarrassed and frustrated with myself.

So yes, I guess I would say my thoughts feel slower, or maybe more clogged up. Not all the time, but enough that I notice it.
Have you had any periods of more than two weeks where you didn't have these thoughts about not wanting to wake up?

No… I don’t think there’s been a stretch that long where it was completely gone. I wish I could say there had been.

It’s not necessarily every morning, and it’s not always loud in my mind, if that makes sense. Some days I wake up and just get on with things, or at least try to. But then it comes back — that thought that it might be easier if I just hadn’t woken up. And that’s really what frightened me enough to ask for help, because it keeps showing up.

I want to be clear, I’m not making a plan to hurt myself. I’m not thinking through how I would do anything. It’s more like this awful, tired thought that comes in when I wake up. But no, I can’t honestly say I’ve had more than two weeks where I haven’t had it at all.
Do you think you've been feeling more sluggish or lethargic physically since your sister passed away?

Yes… yes, I think so. I wouldn’t have described it that way at first, maybe, because I kept thinking of it as just being tired or “not up to things,” but physically, yes, I do feel more weighed down.

Even small errands take so much out of me now. Things that used to be nothing — going to pick something up, stopping at the store, getting papers together for the Cultural Center — I’ll do one of those and feel like I’ve used up the whole day. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because they’re not big tasks. They’re ordinary things.

It feels like my body is moving through thick mud sometimes. Like I can technically do the thing, but everything takes more effort than it should. I’ll stand there with papers spread out on the table, trying to organize them, and it feels like just lifting my arms or walking from one room to another is more work than it ought to be.

So yes, I have felt more sluggish physically since she passed. Not every minute, but enough that I notice it, and it’s made even simple things feel strangely exhausting.
Have you noticed yourself speaking more slowly than usual since your sister passed away?

I’m not really sure about that one. I haven’t especially noticed myself talking more slowly, at least not in the way I notice some other things.

I mean, I may pause more because I’m trying to find what I want to say, or because I lose the thread a little, but I don’t know if my actual speech is slower. No one has said to me, “You’re speaking differently,” or anything like that. And when I’m talking to someone, I’m not always paying attention to my pace, so it’s a little hard for me to judge.

So… I’d say I haven’t noticed a clear change in how fast I speak. If it’s happening, it’s not something I’m very aware of.
Have you been feeling like you need to keep moving or doing something, like pacing back and forth, since your sister passed away?

I don’t think so… not in the sense of pacing or feeling like I have to keep moving all the time.

If anything, I’ve noticed the opposite more, where I end up sitting too long or sort of getting stuck before I start something. But as far as feeling restless in my body — like I need to walk around the room, or I can’t sit still, or I have to keep doing things just to manage the feeling — no, I haven’t really noticed that.

I do sometimes putter, I suppose, like moving a paper from one place to another or fussing with something on the table, but that feels more like not knowing where to begin than a physical urge to keep moving. So… no, I wouldn’t say pacing or that kind of restlessness has been a big thing for me.
Have you been feeling like you have less energy than you used to since your sister passed away?

Yes, definitely. I feel like I have much less energy than I used to.

It’s not just being tired at the end of a busy day, because honestly some of the days aren’t even that busy. It can be something very simple, like going out for one errand, or trying to get the papers together for the Cultural Center, and afterward I feel worn out in a way that seems out of proportion. I’ll think, “Well, that shouldn’t have taken so much out of me,” but it does.

It’s like my body doesn’t have the same reserve it used to. I can still make myself do things, at least some things, but it feels like moving through thick mud. Everything takes more effort, and then I need to sit down or stop. I find myself planning around how much energy something might take, even if it’s a small thing.

So yes… I’d say I have noticeably less energy since she passed away.
Have you been feeling an internal restlessness or a need to be in constant motion since your sister passed away?

No, I don’t think I’ve felt that kind of internal restlessness. I mean, I understand what you’re asking — like a sort of engine running inside, where you feel you have to move or you can’t settle — and I don’t really recognize that in myself.

I may shift around a bit if I’m uncomfortable, or get up and do some small thing, but it doesn’t feel like this constant need to be in motion. I’m not pacing around the house or feeling driven to keep moving. If anything, I tend to sit with things longer than I probably should, but in terms of that restless, keyed-up feeling in my body… no, I haven’t really noticed that since my sister passed away.
Have you been experiencing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning since your sister passed away?

Yes… I think I would have to say it has affected things. I don’t like saying that, because I usually try very hard to keep up with what I’ve agreed to do, especially with the Cultural Center and community things, but I haven’t been functioning quite the way I normally would.

For example, with the Juneteenth budgeting workshop, I had to ask another volunteer to cover parts of the preparation. Normally I would just sit down and work through the materials and make sure everything was in order, but lately I just haven’t been able to keep up with it the way I usually can. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because it’s not that I don’t care about it. I do care. I just couldn’t pull everything together by myself.

And socially, I’ve been turning people down more than usual. Neighbors will invite me over, or friends will ask if I want to stop by or join them for something small, and I find myself saying no or putting it off. Not always in some dramatic way, but enough that I notice it. So yes, it’s caused some real disruption, even if I’m still trying to manage.
How many months have you been experiencing these depressive thoughts and feelings since your sister passed away?

It’s been about a month now. I keep having to stop and count it out because it feels strange — in some ways it feels very recent, and in other ways it feels like it has stretched on much longer — but yes, about a month since my sister died unexpectedly.

That’s really when all of this started. Before that, I wouldn’t say I was feeling like this in the same way. Since she passed, it’s been pretty continuous, not every single minute exactly, but this has been the time period… roughly one month.
Do you feel like these thoughts and feelings have been interfering with your daily life most of the time since your sister passed away?

Yes, I think it has been interfering most of the time, in a practical sense. I still try to do the basic things I’m supposed to do, but I’m not keeping up the way I normally would.

The clearest example is the Juneteenth budgeting workshop. That’s the kind of thing I would usually take seriously and prepare for carefully, but I had to ask another volunteer to cover parts of it because I just couldn’t stay on top of the preparation by myself. That felt very unlike me.

And with people, too… I’ve been saying no more than usual. Neighbors will invite me over, or friends will ask me to come by, and I’ll turn them down or put it off. Not every single time, but more often than I usually would. So yes, it has been getting in the way of my daily life.
Have you been experiencing these depressive thoughts and feelings nearly every day since your sister passed away?

Yes… nearly every day, I’d say. It’s been about a month now, since my sister died unexpectedly, and I don’t think there have really been many days where it hasn’t been there in some form.

Some days it’s more in the background, and I can go through the motions a little better, but it’s still there. And other days it feels much closer to the surface. But since she passed, this has been pretty much the pattern — about a month of these thoughts and feelings being with me almost every day.

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: What scared me enough to ask for help is that I keep having mornings where I think it might be easier if I just didn't wake up, even though I don't have a plan to hurt myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the continuity and duration of thoughts about not wanting to wake up, which directly relates to recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think there’s been a stretch that long where it was completely gone. I wish I could say there had been.

It’s not necessarily every morning, and it’s not always loud in my mind, if that makes sense. Some days I wake up and just get on with things, or at least try to. But then it comes back — that thought that it might be easier if I just hadn’t woken up. And that’s really what frightened me enough to ask for help, because it keeps showing up.

I want to be clear, I’m not making a plan to hurt myself. I’m not thinking through how I would do anything. It’s more like this awful, tired thought that comes in when I wake up. But no, I can’t honestly say I’ve had more than two weeks where I haven’t had it at all.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you think you've been feeling more sluggish or lethargic physically since your sister passed away?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: Even simple errands or getting the papers together for the Cultural Center leave me feeling worn out, like my body is moving through thick mud.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling physically sluggish or lethargic, which most directly matches persistent fatigue and lack of energy.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I think so. I wouldn’t have described it that way at first, maybe, because I kept thinking of it as just being tired or “not up to things,” but physically, yes, I do feel more weighed down.

Even small errands take so much out of me now. Things that used to be nothing — going to pick something up, stopping at the store, getting papers together for the Cultural Center — I’ll do one of those and feel like I’ve used up the whole day. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because they’re not big tasks. They’re ordinary things.

It feels like my body is moving through thick mud sometimes. Like I can technically do the thing, but everything takes more effort than it should. I’ll stand there with papers spread out on the table, trying to organize them, and it feels like just lifting my arms or walking from one room to another is more work than it ought to be.

So yes, I have felt more sluggish physically since she passed. Not every minute, but enough that I notice it, and it’s made even simple things feel strangely exhausting.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself speaking more slowly than usual since your sister passed away?

target_item.reason: The question asks about speaking more slowly, which relates to psychomotor/speech slowing; this is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure about that one. I haven’t especially noticed myself talking more slowly, at least not in the way I notice some other things.

I mean, I may pause more because I’m trying to find what I want to say, or because I lose the thread a little, but I don’t know if my actual speech is slower. No one has said to me, “You’re speaking differently,” or anything like that. And when I’m talking to someone, I’m not always paying attention to my pace, so it’s a little hard for me to judge.

So… I’d say I haven’t noticed a clear change in how fast I speak. If it’s happening, it’s not something I’m very aware of.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation
doctor.question: Have you been feeling like you need to keep moving or doing something, like pacing back and forth, since your sister passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation or physical restlessness, such as pacing or feeling driven to keep moving, and the provided symptom profile does not include an item for that symptom.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in the sense of pacing or feeling like I have to keep moving all the time.

If anything, I’ve noticed the opposite more, where I end up sitting too long or sort of getting stuck before I start something. But as far as feeling restless in my body — like I need to walk around the room, or I can’t sit still, or I have to keep doing things just to manage the feeling — no, I haven’t really noticed that.

I do sometimes putter, I suppose, like moving a paper from one place to another or fussing with something on the table, but that feels more like not knowing where to begin than a physical urge to keep moving. So… no, I wouldn’t say pacing or that kind of restlessness has been a big thing for me.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of loss of energy
doctor.question: Have you been feeling like you have less energy than you used to since your sister passed away?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: Even simple errands or getting the papers together for the Cultural Center leave me feeling worn out, like my body is moving through thick mud.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about having less energy than usual, which matches the fatigue symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. I feel like I have much less energy than I used to.

It’s not just being tired at the end of a busy day, because honestly some of the days aren’t even that busy. It can be something very simple, like going out for one errand, or trying to get the papers together for the Cultural Center, and afterward I feel worn out in a way that seems out of proportion. I’ll think, “Well, that shouldn’t have taken so much out of me,” but it does.

It’s like my body doesn’t have the same reserve it used to. I can still make myself do things, at least some things, but it feels like moving through thick mud. Everything takes more effort, and then I need to sit down or stop. I find myself planning around how much energy something might take, even if it’s a small thing.

So yes… I’d say I have noticeably less energy since she passed away.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation
doctor.question: Have you been feeling an internal restlessness or a need to be in constant motion since your sister passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about internal restlessness or a need for constant motion, which relates to psychomotor agitation. That symptom is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think I’ve felt that kind of internal restlessness. I mean, I understand what you’re asking — like a sort of engine running inside, where you feel you have to move or you can’t settle — and I don’t really recognize that in myself.

I may shift around a bit if I’m uncomfortable, or get up and do some small thing, but it doesn’t feel like this constant need to be in motion. I’m not pacing around the house or feeling driven to keep moving. If anything, I tend to sit with things longer than I probably should, but in terms of that restless, keyed-up feeling in my body… no, I haven’t really noticed that since my sister passed away.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive symptoms to differentiate between F33.1 and F33.2
doctor.question: Have you been experiencing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning since your sister passed away?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I have had to ask another volunteer to cover parts of the Juneteenth budgeting workshop because I cannot keep up with the preparation the way I normally would, and I have been turning down neighbors and friends more than usual.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, which matches the Functional Impairment profile.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think I would have to say it has affected things. I don’t like saying that, because I usually try very hard to keep up with what I’ve agreed to do, especially with the Cultural Center and community things, but I haven’t been functioning quite the way I normally would.

For example, with the Juneteenth budgeting workshop, I had to ask another volunteer to cover parts of the preparation. Normally I would just sit down and work through the materials and make sure everything was in order, but lately I just haven’t been able to keep up with it the way I usually can. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because it’s not that I don’t care about it. I do care. I just couldn’t pull everything together by myself.

And socially, I’ve been turning people down more than usual. Neighbors will invite me over, or friends will ask if I want to stop by or join them for something small, and I find myself saying no or putting it off. Not always in some dramatic way, but enough that I notice it. So yes, it’s caused some real disruption, even if I’m still trying to manage.

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the patient's depressive symptoms to differentiate between F33.1 and F33.2
doctor.question: How many months have you been experiencing these depressive thoughts and feelings since your sister passed away?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a month, since my sister died unexpectedly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how many months the depressive thoughts and feelings have been present since the sister passed away, which directly matches the duration item.

patient.answer:
It’s been about a month now. I keep having to stop and count it out because it feels strange — in some ways it feels very recent, and in other ways it feels like it has stretched on much longer — but yes, about a month since my sister died unexpectedly.

That’s really when all of this started. Before that, I wouldn’t say I was feeling like this in the same way. Since she passed, it’s been pretty continuous, not every single minute exactly, but this has been the time period… roughly one month.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive episode
doctor.question: Do you feel like these thoughts and feelings have been interfering with your daily life most of the time since your sister passed away?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I have had to ask another volunteer to cover parts of the Juneteenth budgeting workshop because I cannot keep up with the preparation the way I normally would, and I have been turning down neighbors and friends more than usual.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the depressive thoughts and feelings have been interfering with daily life, which directly matches functional impairment in social and community responsibilities.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think it has been interfering most of the time, in a practical sense. I still try to do the basic things I’m supposed to do, but I’m not keeping up the way I normally would.

The clearest example is the Juneteenth budgeting workshop. That’s the kind of thing I would usually take seriously and prepare for carefully, but I had to ask another volunteer to cover parts of it because I just couldn’t stay on top of the preparation by myself. That felt very unlike me.

And with people, too… I’ve been saying no more than usual. Neighbors will invite me over, or friends will ask me to come by, and I’ll turn them down or put it off. Not every single time, but more often than I usually would. So yes, it has been getting in the way of my daily life.

doctor.intent: determine the severity of depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you been experiencing these depressive thoughts and feelings nearly every day since your sister passed away?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a month, since my sister died unexpectedly.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the time course and near-daily persistence of the depressive thoughts and feelings since the sister's death, which is best matched by the duration item.

patient.answer:
Yes… nearly every day, I’d say. It’s been about a month now, since my sister died unexpectedly, and I don’t think there have really been many days where it hasn’t been there in some form.

Some days it’s more in the background, and I can go through the motions a little better, but it’s still there. And other days it feels much closer to the surface. But since she passed, this has been pretty much the pattern — about a month of these thoughts and feelings being with me almost every day.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms, including persistent depressive thoughts, loss of interest in activities, significant weight loss, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, and diminished ability to think or concentrate, have been present for about a month since a significant traumatic event (the death of their sister). These symptoms have caused significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
